title: Demyan's Fish Soup
text:
Demyan had invited his neighbor Foka to dinner and served him a pot of fish soup, the clear Russian ukha. It was very good soup, and Demyan was very proud of it.

"Come, dear friend, have another plate," he said. "Just look at it, a fine bream, and here are the giblets, and a bit of sturgeon. Eat, eat, do me the favor." Foka had already eaten one plate. He ate a second. Demyan filled it again. "Another spoonful, neighbor, it is made just for you. Wife, come and bow to our guest so he will eat more."

Poor Foka was sweating. He had eaten three plates and could not swallow another drop, but he did not want to offend his host. Demyan kept talking, kept praising, kept filling the plate, and would not hear a refusal.

At last Foka could bear no more. He seized his belt and his hat, jumped up, and fled out of the house without a word of goodbye. And from that day on he never set foot in Demyan's house again.

Krylov aimed the fable at a writer who forces his works on his listeners, but in Russian "Demyan's soup" has become a phrase for any kindness pressed on someone until it becomes a burden.
lesson: Generosity should serve the other person, not your own wish to be thanked. When someone says they have had enough, believe them.
source: Ivan Krylov, Fables, Demyan's Fish Soup (Demyanova ukha)
